label: explain-bm-contract
one_line: We are checking what a printed, damp-air-bending building part must pass, who might pay for it, and who owns the ideas.
what: We want to offer a London design studio a small proof of concept. It is a printed strip made of two plastic layers. One layer swells in damp air and the other does not, so the strip curls. A curling strip could open or close a shade with no motor. Before building it, eight research helpers read the rules, safety sheets, grant lists, patents and past studies. This page sums up what they found. It covers the contract side: what the part must pass, what it costs to handle, who pays, and who owns what. We are not selling a finished building product. We are planning a sample plus a rule for how to design it.
why: Many clever building ideas fail on boring questions. Will it burn? Is it safe to print? Who pays? Does someone already own the idea? Answering these first saves months of work. It also stops us from saying things we cannot prove. For example, nobody has yet measured an energy saving from a damp-air shade. The best real example only measured how much shade it made. A fair offer to the studio should say that plainly. It should offer measurements the studio lacks, not promises.

steps.text: Read the English building rules. Find out which parts of a tall building must be almost non-burning.
steps.picture: Checking the rulebook of a sport before you sign up a team.

steps.text: Check what burn data the printer maker publishes. Compare it with what the rules ask for.
steps.picture: Asking whether your driving test covers the road you plan to use.

steps.text: Look for any test standard for parts that bend in damp air. Note what researchers do instead.
steps.picture: Finding no recipe in any cookbook, so reading how other cooks improvised.

steps.text: Compare the heat bending and the damp bending of the two layers. Both can curl the strip.
steps.picture: A metal thermostat strip that bends when warm, mixed up with a wet paper strip that curls.

steps.text: Read the safety sheets for the printing liquids and the waste rules. List what to avoid.
steps.picture: Reading the label on a strong glue before opening the tin.

steps.text: Search grant lists and the studio's own pages. See who pays for what, and when.
steps.picture: Reading a train timetable to see which trains run and which are cancelled.

steps.text: Scan patent records for ideas close to ours. Note which are live and which have lapsed.
steps.picture: Walking a fence line to see which plots are already claimed.

steps.text: Re-run the key sums and spot checks. A second set of readers rechecked the main claims.
steps.picture: Having a friend recount the change at a till.

wrong_if: Our bet, written down before looking: nobody will pay for the rule alone, and no printed resin will pass the fire rules for tall homes. We would be wrong if a firm showed it pays for design rules alone. We would also be wrong if a printed resin earned the top fire class. Neither was found. We would also be wrong if a damp-air shade had a measured energy saving. The helpers searched and found none, but they could not search everywhere.
could_go_wrong: The helpers searched limited sources, so 'nobody has done this' may simply mean 'we did not find it'.
The patent scan was only partly checked: two key patent claims could not be re-read by the checkers, so we leave them out.
The swelling figure for one flexible resin came from a scrambled data sheet and has not been re-measured in damp air.
The damp-air strip may bend more from heat than from damp, which could hide the effect we want to show.
The grant lists change fast, and most European ones need an applicant based in Europe.
We do not know whether the team is a company or a university group, and that decides which grants fit.
A patent lawyer has not looked at anything, so ownership questions are open.
The studio prints with robot arms and plant plastic, not with resin or powder, so our samples only prove the shape idea.

questions.a: Each helper saved the pages it read and wrote down exact quotes. A second set of readers then rechecked the main claims. We only use claims they could confirm, in full or in part. Several others are listed under 'left out'.

We have not tested any printed strip yet. We did not read paid standards or the full text of some papers. We did not check Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland. No lawyer or fire engineer has reviewed this.

questions.q: Could a printed plastic part be used as a shade on a tall block of flats in England?
questions.a: Probably not. For homes with a floor at 18 metres or higher, outer wall parts must be nearly non-burning. That is roughly six floors up. Shading slats are not exempt. Shading under 4.5 metres from the ground falls outside that rule.

questions.q: Can we say the part is fire safe?
questions.a: No. A real fire class needs large test pieces, so a desk print cannot be rated. The printer maker publishes only a small plastic burn rating, and the building rules do not use it.

Clients pay for finished installations. Public grants pay for early proof work. Window and shade makers join public projects but offer help, not cash. We found nobody who pays for a design rule alone, though we may have missed some.

questions.q: Is the idea patented by someone else?
questions.a: Many nearby ideas are patented, so we cannot claim 'a plate that curls in damp air'. Some patents on wood versions are narrow. The first scan found nothing pairing a computer-checked proof with print design, but a lawyer must confirm that.

With care, yes. All 14 resin sheets checked mark the liquid as a skin allergy risk. Two resins also carry a warning for harm to unborn children, so we would leave those out of any public sample. Gloves, goggles and fresh air are required.

questions.q: Can we call it green or recyclable?
questions.a: No. The printer maker says cured resin and used powder cannot be recycled. It calls one powder bio-based but gives no percentage. New EU rules limit vague claims like 'biobased' from 27 September 2026.

check_yourself.expect: The text 'Smart grants are now closed for new applications'.

check_yourself.what: Check that the big US materials grant runs only every second year, and that the last window was early 2025.
check_yourself.expect: 'January 21, 2025 - February 04, 2025' and 'competitions biennially in odd-numbered years'.

check_yourself.what: Recompute the heat-versus-damp bending sums and the test-length sums.
check_yourself.expect: Difference in expansion 113.6 to 127.2 micrometres per metre per degree; thermal strain 0.454 % to 0.509 % over 40 K; 170 cycles = 1020 hours = 42.5 days.

check_yourself.what: Confirm the small-scale burn rating is absent from the English fire guide.
Check the swelling of the flexible resin in water by word position in the data sheet.
Re-run the humidity-versus-shade-need check for nine cities.
check_yourself.expect: Singapore 0.98 (shade mostly open in hours when shade is wanted), Madrid 0.95, Houston 0.38.

left_out: Patent US 11155025 B2 (MIT and Stratasys) status and expiry: the checkers could not load the patent pages, so it is unconfirmed.
The claim that no patent pairs a theorem prover with material or print design: the checkers could not reach the search pages.
The claim that the bilayer ratio optimum appears in an older patent text citing Timoshenko: the page could not be fetched.
Sloan and Holcim funder status: not checked by the verifiers.

'Smart grants closed, so Knowledge Transfer Partnerships, small-business grants and Royce are the live routes': only the closure is confirmed; the agent's own file says KTP round one is closed and Royce eligibility was not read.
'Only the Graham grant is open' among private funders: a second Graham grant (15 Nov 2026) is also open, so the claim is not safe.
'The only flexible resin that swells enough' and 'humid-air constants unpublished': not shown by the verifier.
'No standard exists' for damp-responsive parts and 'only UL 94 is published': absence claims that could not be proved.
'Nine of 25 data sheets give a burn rating': the count was not rechecked.
The 0.2 percent damp-swelling estimate: it is the agent's own and cannot be checked here.
'The only structural test on any practice page is one pull test': wrong, as other pages report load tests.
'No energy or comfort benefit exists anywhere' for damp-driven shades, and 'humidity vents are the only element with in-service numbers': sweeping absence claims; we say only that none was found.
'Mycelium has no verified fire class' as a blanket statement: sources support only 'rarely tested'.
Client claims for Neko Health, COS and Buro Happold, and 'no fees published': not opened by the verifiers.
'No facade maker pays outsiders for material research' and the Formlabs in-kind claim: negative findings not checked.
